name: Irrigation
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.methods:
Pakistan's irrigation sources are rivers, canals, tubewells and rain. The Indus system has 3 big reservoirs, 19 barrages, 12 link canals, 45 main canals and about 107,000 watercourses (about 140 million acre-feet a year). About 90 percent of the country's water goes to agriculture, but about 80 percent of that is lost to poor irrigation and distribution.
Drip irrigation: a pipe network with holes right next to each plant, giving water drop by drop (5 to 10 litres per hour per dripper) and fertilizer straight to the roots. Saves about 70 percent water and raises yield 20 to 30 percent. Parts: main pipe, sub-main pipe, emitters, pump, filter, fertilizer unit and water meter. Suits vegetables (tomato, onion, cucumber, chilli), orchards (peach, grape, olive) and high-value crops (cotton, sugarcane, maize). Keep the dripper holes from clogging. Micro-tube (sub-surface) drip lasts longer and can run on solar; a tank 6 feet above ground can gravity-water a 5-acre orchard.
Bubbler irrigation: water is sprayed in a ring around each plant; for big trees or high-water plants. Parts: pump, control head, main and sub-main pipes, laterals, drippers and bubblers.
Sprinklers: spray water like rain and can apply fertilizer. Hand-move lateral: suits all crops and uneven land, but needs more labour and joints can leak. Gun sprinkler: for large rectangular fields and orchards, low starting cost, but not for windy areas, the force can damage soil or crop, and it needs more energy. Permanent sprinkler: for orchards, lawns and ornamental plants, automatic, less labour, but costly to set up. Centre pivot: rotates in a circle, even watering, automatic, but costly and misses field corners; not for land with trees. Linear move: moves back and forth, waters edges too, but costly and only for rectangular fields.
Ridge and furrow: water runs in narrow furrows between crop rows, wetting less area and saving water; used for vegetables, cotton, maize and sugarcane, and now for wheat too.
Gated pipe: a surface pipe with small gates replaces the earthen watercourse; open or close gates to control water. Saves water; used with furrows or basins.
Siphon tube: a curved plastic pipe filled with water moves water from the watercourse to the field without cutting the bank; easy to move.
Pipe nakka: a concrete outlet with a pipe; no bricks or cement needed, cheap, farmer can install it, stops leaks from earthen outlets, durable and movable.
Rainwater harvesting: micro-catchments are shaped basins with slopes and channels that collect rain around each plant (best on slopes up to 5 percent, fertile land free of waterlogging and salinity, with a 3:1 ratio of catchment to planted area). Rooftop harvesting stores rain from roofs in a tank for home and small-scale irrigation.
Tunnel farming: a frame of iron pipes or bamboo for off-season vegetables (tomato, cucumber, chilli). Flood irrigation in a tunnel raises humidity and disease; drip keeps water at the plant. Plastic mulch with drip controls disease and weeds and stops evaporation.
Measuring soil moisture removes guesswork: tensiometer (ceramic cup and pressure gauge), electrical moisture meter, gypsum block, TDR meter, FullStop (a simple float device that shows when the field needs water) and atmometer (measures evaporation).
Laser land levelling (introduced by the Punjab Agriculture Department in 1985): a transmitter sends a laser beam and a receiver on the tractor scraper keeps it level automatically. First reduce level differences to about 6 inches with an ordinary scraper to keep costs down.
aspects.benefits:
Drip: about 70 percent water saving, 20 to 30 percent more yield (20 to 100 percent in Punjab surveys), 20 to 35 percent lower production cost, better quality, 30 percent less labour for watering, suits uneven land with no levelling cost, steady water on sandy soil, fertilizer efficiency of 30 to 95 percent, and fewer weeds because soil between plants stays dry. Keeps the ideal soil moisture (about 25 percent water, 25 percent air), so roots feed easily. Reduces salts near the roots.
Solar-powered drip: no fuel or running cost, no trouble during power cuts, fewer poles and wires, and with a battery it can run at night.
Bubbler: less water lost on the way, fertilizer not wasted, no levelling needed, fewer weeds, low cost.
Micro-catchments: more water to the plant with little work, simple and cheap to build, better soil absorption, less waterlogging and salinity. For olive plants: 3 extra irrigations instead of 6, 65 percent water saving, cost 15 rupees per plant instead of 50.
Laser levelling: up to 50 percent water saving, up to 25 percent more yield, 42 percent more irrigated area, 35 to 40 percent higher cropping intensity, 15 to 35 percent better fertilizer efficiency, up to 42 percent less waterlogging and salinity, 60 percent less land under bunds and watercourses, and less erosion. Uneven land wastes 20 to 25 percent of irrigation water; low spots lose nutrients and high spots build up salts.
Raised beds or ridges for wheat save up to 30 percent water and prevent lodging.
aspects.economics:
Pakistan is ranked third among countries facing severe water shortage (IMF); UNDP and PCRWR warned of a severe water crisis. About 67 percent of the economy depends on agriculture.
Costs (rates given in the KB): drip system 50,000 to 100,000 rupees per acre, depending on field and crop. Solar panels 90 to 200 rupees per watt depending on quality. Bubbler system 135,000 to 140,000 rupees per acre, paid back in one to two years from income; it saves 40 to 50 percent water and raises yield 25 to 40 percent compared with flood irrigation.
